sections.heading: Asking mercy for the whole record of my life
sections.text: Merciful Lord, I come to you without excuses. Please forgive the sins of today, this week, this year, and all the years behind me. Forgive what I did when I was young, what I did in the middle of life, and what I have done as I have grown older. Forgive the wrong things I chose, and the good things I left undone. Nothing in my story is hidden from you, and I need mercy over all of it.
theological_themes: Sin as both wrongdoing and neglected obedience
God’s complete knowledge of the whole life

scripture_references.connection: John teaches believers to be honest about sin rather than deny it, and to come to God for cleansing. This grounds the prayer’s direct request for pardon across the whole life.
James shows that sin includes failing to do the good we know we should do. That supports the prayer’s confession of both committed sins and neglected duties.

sections.heading: Confessing what has come out of my heart
sections.text: Forgive the bitterness, irritability, and anger that have lived in me and spilled out of me. Forgive the sins of my mouth, my habits, and the way I move through the world. Forgive my hard heart, my unbelief, my pride, and the times I acted confident in myself instead of dependent on you.
theological_themes: Need for inward renewal, not merely outward improvement

scripture_references.connection: Jesus locates defiling sin in the human heart, not merely in outward actions. This supports confessing temper, pride, unbelief, speech, and conduct as symptoms of a deeper problem within.
Paul connects speech, anger, bitterness, and forgiveness in the life of a Christian. This passage illuminates the prayer’s confession of harsh attitudes and damaging words.

sections.heading: Confessing failures to honor Christ and love people
sections.text: Forgive me for the ways I have failed people who needed my care, honesty, prayers, or witness. Forgive me for being timid when I should have stood clearly with Christ. Forgive me for being quiet about his worth when I should have gladly honored him. Forgive me for making your name look small or unattractive by the way I lived.
theological_themes: Responsibility to love and serve others
God’s glory reflected or dishonored by his people

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that his disciples’ visible lives should lead others to glorify the Father. This supports confessing the ways one’s conduct can either honor or dishonor God before others.
Paul urges Timothy not to be ashamed of testimony about Christ, but to rely on God’s power. This bears directly on the prayer’s confession of cowardice or lack of open zeal for Christ.

sections.heading: Confessing dishonesty, impurity, and misuse of what you gave me
sections.text: Forgive every false, unfair, or misleading thing in my dealings with others. Forgive impurity in what I have thought, said, and done. Forgive my greed, which treats created things as if they could take your place. Forgive the ways I have clung too tightly to money and possessions, wasted them carelessly, or used them as though they were mine first and not gifts from you to be used for your glory.
theological_themes: Purity of thought, speech, and action

scripture_references.connection: Paul names sexual impurity, evil desire, covetousness, lying, and the putting off of the old self together. This passage strongly supports the prayer’s confession of impurity, greed, and dishonesty.

Paul warns believers not to set their hopes on riches, but to receive and use what God gives for generosity and good works. This connects to confessing both hoarding and waste as failures of stewardship.

sections.heading: Confessing sin in ordinary places and spiritual things
sections.text: Forgive what I have done in secret, at home, in my work, in my rest, and around other people. Forgive the sins mixed into my reading of Scripture, and the sin of neglecting your Word altogether. Forgive prayers I offered without reverence or attention, and prayers I withheld because my heart was cold. Forgive the time I have wasted and the moments I treated as though they did not belong to you.
theological_themes: God sees private and public life
The need for reverence in prayer and Scripture
Time as a gift entrusted by God

scripture_references.connection: Hebrews presents God’s Word as exposing the heart, and God himself as the one before whom nothing is hidden. This supports confessing sin not only in obvious actions but even in religious practices and hidden motives.
Paul calls believers to walk wisely and make careful use of time because the days are evil. This illuminates the confession of misspent time and careless living.

sections.heading: Confessing weakness in temptation and resistance to your Spirit
sections.text: Forgive me for giving in to the devil’s schemes, for leaving the door open to temptation, and for being careless when I knew danger was close. Forgive me for resisting the Holy Spirit’s warnings, ignoring the light you had already given me, and pushing past conscience when it was telling the truth. Forgive every sin against your law of love.
theological_themes: Sin against known truth and conscience

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the Christian life as involving real spiritual opposition and calls believers to stand in the Lord’s strength. This supports the prayer’s confession of carelessness toward temptation and the devil’s schemes.
Paul warns believers not to quench the Spirit and to discern and hold fast to what is good. This relates closely to confessing resistance to the Spirit’s work and neglect of God-given warnings.
Paul teaches that love fulfills the law. This grounds the prayer’s final confession of sin as a violation of God’s command to love.

sections.heading: Asking forgiveness for what I see and what I do not see
sections.text: Lord, forgive all my sins: the ones I know and the ones I do not recognize; the ones I feel deeply and the ones I have grown numb to; the ones I have confessed and the ones I have not yet named; the ones I remember and the ones I have forgotten. Please hear me. And because you are merciful, forgive me.
theological_themes: Confidence that God hears repentant prayer

scripture_references.connection: David asks God for cleansing from hidden faults as well as protection from willful sin. This directly supports asking forgiveness for sins that are unknown, forgotten, or not fully felt.
David appeals to God’s steadfast love and mercy while taking responsibility for sin before God. This mirrors the prayer’s posture of humble confession and plea for pardon.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original assumes a strongly Puritan practice of detailed self-examination, including confession of sins that may be unfelt, forgotten, or not yet consciously identified. This is biblically supportable, but some readers may find it spiritually intense or pastorally heavy if separated from the assurance of the gospel.
The reference to Satan’s schemes reflects a traditional and biblical view of personal spiritual evil; it was retained without reducing temptation to merely psychological struggle.

The phrase about being unfaithful to 'the souls of men' is culturally older language and can sound impersonal today; it has been rendered as failure in care, prayer, honesty, and witness toward people.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted 'sins of omission and commission' as both wrong actions chosen and good duties neglected, preserving the original’s moral breadth without using technical language.

I rendered 'want of bold decision in the cause of Christ' and 'deficiency in outspoken zeal for his glory' as timidity in standing with Christ and reluctance to honor him openly, rather than as a demand for loudness or personality-driven activism.

I treated the references to hoarding, squandering, and not consecrating substance to God as a confession about stewardship of money and possessions, not as a blanket condemnation of saving or ordinary enjoyment.

I kept the original’s comprehensive final sweep—known and unknown, felt and unfelt, confessed and unconfessed, remembered and forgotten—because it is central to the prayer’s theology of God’s full knowledge and the believer’s need for mercy.
